title-group.article-title: Celafolin A-1 Ameliorates Subretinal Fibrosis via Inhibition of Crystallin Alpha B in a Laser-Induced Choroidal Neovascularization Mouse Model

abstract.p: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a leading cause of blindness in people over 65 years old. Anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) therapy is the first-line treatment for neovascular AMD (nAMD); however, fibrosis remains an unmet medical need due to the lack of effective medications. This study evaluated eight natural products from Celastrus orbiculatus, which has been reported to have anti-inflammatory effects, for their effects on the fibrotic pathological process as well as choroidal neovascularization (CNV). We investigated the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values of these compounds on VEGF and alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA, a fibrosis marker) expression-induced by human acute monocytic cell (THP-1) conditioned media in retinal pigment epithelium cells (ARPE-19). Four compounds reduced both VEGF and α-SMA at 10 μM, with three—Celafolin A-1, COFH5645, and COFH543435—showing the highest potency. Intravitreal injections of the compound in a mouse model of CNV induced by laser photocoagulation confirmed its efficacy. Celafolin A-1 significantly reduced α-SMA and VEGF expression and decreased hyper-reflective lesions and CNV areas. Binding affinity measurements using biolayer interferometry identified an interaction between Celafolin A-1 and crystallin alpha B (Cryab), a protein involved in stress responses and fibrosis. Celafolin A-1 reduced the expression levels of Cryab as well as its phosphorylated form at Ser45, indicating that its mechanism involves the regulation of Cryab phosphorylation. Taken together, Celafolin A-1 exhibits dual inhibitory effects on VEGF and fibrosis, suggesting it as a candidate for the treatment of nAMD.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD) is the leading cause of irreversible blindness in the elderly population (Klaver et al., 1998). This disease is characterized by the formation of abnormal blood vessels in the subretinal area (Evans, 2001), leading to vascular leakage, hemorrhage, and the development of choroidal neovascularization (CNV) (Wang et al., 2007). CNV, a critical pathological feature of nAMD, results in severe visual impairment due to the leakage and bleeding of newly formed vessels, causing damage to the macula, the central part of the retina. Anti-VEGF pharmaceutical products have been successfully used to treat nAMD (Rosenfeld et al., 2006). These therapies target vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), a key molecule involved in the formation and maintenance of abnormal blood vessels.

By inhibiting VEGF, these treatments can reduce CNV and slow the progression of nAMD. However, despite the efficacy of anti-VEGF therapies in managing neovascularization, some patients develop subretinal fibrosis as a complication (Daniel et al., 2014). Subretinal fibrosis leads to permanent scarring beneath the retina, further impairing vision. The development of CNV triggers subretinal fibrosis, leading to bleeding and an inflammatory response (Lambert et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2007). Various cell types, such as fibroblasts, immune cells, and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, are involved in this pathological process (Lambert et al., 2016). RPE cells are crucial in maintaining retinal function; however, under pathological conditions, they produce VEGF and express several fibrosis markers dependent on the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) process (Schwesinger et al., 2001; Tamiya et al., 2010). EMT in RPE cells contributes to the fibrotic response observed in nAMD, further complicating its treatment.

To date, there are no effective medications specifically targeting fibrosis in nAMD treatment. To address this issue, we analyzed eight natural products isolated from Celastrus orbiculatus (C. orbiculatus) and identified compounds with potential for treating nAMD through their anti-neovascular and anti-fibrotic actions. C. orbiculatus is a plant known for its diverse pharmacological activities, including antitumor, antitubercular, immunosuppressive, and anti-inflammatory effects (Qian et al., 2012). It has been reported that C. orbiculatus has anti-inflammatory activity through the inhibition of nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) (Jin et al., 2002). Furthermore, C. orbiculatus has been reported to inhibit the NF-κB pathway as well as VEGF expression (Jin et al., 2002; Qian et al., 2012) and inhibit EMT (Wang et al., 2023), a critical process that contributes to both neovascularization and fibrosis. Based on these findings, we hypothesized that compounds derived from this plant could directly suppress the key pathological mechanisms of nAMD such as neovascularization and fibrosis. NF-κB is a transcription factor that, when activated, promotes VEGF expression (Kiriakidis et al., 2003), linking inflammation to neovascularization. Despite its known pharmacological properties, the effects of C. orbiculatus on nAMD had not been previously investigated. This study aims to evaluate the potential of C. orbiculatus-derived compounds in treating the fibrotic process of nAMD. We investigated the effects of Celafolin A-1 on the expression of VEGF and fibrosis markers such as alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) and collagen type I (collagen I) in ARPE-19 cells, a human retinal pigment epithelial cell line commonly used in retinal research. Additionally, we assessed the anti-neovascularization activity of Celafolin A-1 by measuring the CNV area in a mouse model of nAMD following administration.

To elucidate the possible mechanisms underlying the anti-fibrotic activity of Celafolin A-1, we examined its effects on crystallin alpha B (Cryab) expression. Cryab is a small heat shock protein that interacts with VEGF and α-SMA (Kase et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2022). Cryab plays a crucial role in preventing apoptosis, protecting cells, interacting with proteasomes, and functioning as a molecular chaperone (Andley, 2007). Moreover, Cryab expression is upregulated during angiogenesis (Dimberg et al., 2008) and is associated with fibrosis (Bellaye et al., 2014) and inflammation (Guo et al., 2019). Our previous study has suggested that natural compounds, such as alpinumisoflavone (AIF), may inhibit nAMD pathological processes via interaction with Cryab (Yu et al., 2022). Cryab’s role in cellular stress responses, including heat, oxidation, and elevated intracellular calcium levels, is mediated through its phosphorylation (Ito et al., 1997). In the lens, Cryab phosphorylation increases with age, and phosphorylated Cryab (p-Cryab) regulates the activity of chaperones (Ecroyd et al., 2007).

Therefore, we investigated the inhibitory effect of Celafolin A-1 on the pathophysiology of Cryab, aiming to provide a novel therapeutic approach for nAMD that addresses both neovascularization and fibrosis. Through this research, we aim to contribute to the development of possible treatments for nAMD, addressing the limitations of current therapies and improving patient outcomes.

sec.title: MATERIALS AND METHODS
Ethics statement
sec.p: Eight-week-old male C57BL/6N mice, purchased from DBL (Chungbuk, Korea), were maintained under standard conditions (temperature: 23 ± 2°C, humidity: 50 ± 5%) with a controlled 12-h light-dark cycle (light on 08:00 to 20:00). Four to five mice were housed per cage and provided ad libitum access to food and water. All mouse experiments were approved by the Animal Care Committee of Chungbuk National University, Cheongju, Korea (CBNUA-2029-22-01). The animals were handled following the Association for Research in Vision and Ophthalmology (ARVO) Statement on the Use of Animals in Ophthalmic and Vision Research, and this study was conducted in strict accordance with the recommendations of the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals from the National Institutes of Health.

sec.title: Cell culture
sec.p: ARPE-19 cells (ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA) were cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM, Gibco, Waltham, MA, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and 1% anti-biotic-anti-mycotic (100 units/mL, Gibco, Waltham, MA, USA) under at 37°C and 5% CO2 in a humidified incubator. The medium was changed every other day.

THP-1 monocytes are differentiated into macrophage-like cells by overnight incubation with 200 ng/mL of phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA, Sigma-Aldrich, St Louis, MO, USA). Following differentiation, the cells were stimulated with 1 μg/mL lipopoly-saccharide (LPS, Sigma-Aldrich) in RPMI-1640 for 24 h. The supernatants of these cells were obtained as THP-1 conditioned medium (TCM).

sec.title: In vitro model and test compounds activity screening
sec.p: LPS-stimulated THP-1 cells were used to produce the TCM. ARPE-19 cells were seeded in 96-well black plates at a density of 1×104 cells/well. Two days later, to establish a TCM-induced pathological model mimicking the inflammatory and angiogenic microenvironment, ARPE-19 cells were treated with TCM or the test compounds in TCM for 3 h, and VEGF and α-SMA expression was analyzed. The eight natural products previously listed were assessed, and bevacizumab was used as a positive control. Bevacizumab was treated at 17 μM (2,500 μg/mL), while the test compounds were treated at 10 μM (5.466 μg/mL). The IC50 values were determined from a dose-dependent graph. Thereafter, the cells were treated with 17 μM, 1.7 μM, 170 nM, 17 nM, 1.7 nM, 170 pM, 17 pM, 1.7 pM, 0.17 pM, and 0.017 pM of bevacizumab and 1 mM, 100 μM, 10 μM, 1 μM, 100 nM, 10 nM, 1 nM, 100 pM, 10 pM, and 1 pM of Celafolin A-1 to compare their effectivity. Immunofluorescence was then performed, as described below. The IC50 values were determined using GraphPad Prism 5.

sec.title: Immunofluorescence
sec.p: For the immunofluorescence analysis, ARPE-19 cells were fixed for 20 min with 4% paraformaldehyde, followed by permeabilization with 0.2% Triton X-100 in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS; Life Technologies, Carlsbad, CA, USA) for 15 min. Thereafter, the cells were blocked with 5% BSA for 1 h. Cells were stained with α-SMA (ab5694, 1:300; Abcam, Cambridge, UK) and VEGF (SC-7269, 1:300; Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Dallas, TX, USA) overnight at 4°C. Subsequently, cellular specimens were subjected to a 2-h incubation period with goat anti-rabbit IgG labeled with Alexa Fluor® 568 (ab175471, 1:500; Abcam, Cambridge, UK) or goat anti-mouse IgG labeled with Alexa Fluor® 488 (ab150113, 1:500; Abcam, Cambridge, UK). The fluorescence intensity was measured using a FlexStation 3 Multi-Mode Microplate Reader (Molecular Devices, Sunnyvale, CA, USA).

sec.title: In vivo CNV model and compounds treatment
sec.p: The laser-induced CNV mouse model is commonly used to study nAMD (Lambert et al., 2013; Ryan, 1979). All procedures were conducted with the animals anesthetized via an intraperitoneal injection of 1.2% avertin. Pupils were dilated using a combination of 0.5% tropicamide and 0.5% phenylephrine (Mydrin-P; Santen, Osaka, Japan). Each animal underwent laser photocoagulation at three points on the binocular retina, maintaining careful avoidance of blood vessels. Laser spots were created with a spot diameter of 45 μm using the 78 diopters lens (VOLK, Mentor, OH, USA), 300 mW power, and 100 ms pulse duration employing a laser indirect ophthalmoscope (OcuLight® GL (Green 532 nm Laser), IRIDEX, Mountain View, CA, USA). Before intravitreal injection, a 30-gauge needle was meticulously used to puncture the intravitreal cavity, ensuring it did not touch the lens at the edge. Subsequently, mice received intravitreal injections at the identical puncture site using a 32-gauge needle connected to a 5 μL Hamilton microsyringe (Hamilton, Reno, NV, USA) as follows: 1 μL dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), Celafolin A-1 (5 μg in 1 μL DMSO), COFH5645 (5 μg in 1 μL DMSO), or COFH543435 (5 μg in 1 μL DMSO). The dose was determined based on the in vitro IC50 values. A week later, all mice used in this study were euthanized using CO2 inhalation. The CO2 was gradually introduced into the euthanasia chamber to minimize distress.

sec.title: Optical coherence tomography (OCT)
sec.p: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is a noninvasive imaging technique that enables in vivo cross-sectional visualization of the retina (Bouma et al., 2022). The mice were subjected to experiments seven days after laser photocoagulation. For all procedures, the animals were anesthetized via an intraperitoneal injection of 1.2% avertin. The pupils were dilated using a combination of 0.5% tropicamide and 0.5% phenylephrine (Mydrin-P; Santen). OCT imaging was performed using an OCT system (Eyemera OCT, IISCIENCE, San Jose, CA, USA). Retinal OCT scans were performed in the vertical plane with the laser spot at the center. Manual delineation was used to outline the inner border of the lesion and was used to measure the cross-sectional area of the lesion.

sec.title: Isolectin B4 staining of CNV lesions
sec.p: A previously reported isolectin B4 staining protocol, with slight modifications, was used (Léger et al., 2019). Briefly, seven days after laser photocoagulation, the mice were euthanized. Residual fat, muscle, episcleral membrane, and optic nerve tissue were excised. The cornea and anterior sclera were dissected via an incision just anterior to the equator, using microdissection scissors. Subsequently, the lens, iris, vitreous, and neurosensory retinas were removed. After blocking with PBS containing 5% goat serum and 0.1% Triton X-100 for 1 hour at room temperature, fixed cells were incubated overnight at 4°C with Alexa Fluor 594-conjugated Griffonia simplicifolia isolectin B4 in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) containing 5% goat serum, 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA), and 0.5% Triton X-100. Following three washes with PBS (5 minutes each), the posterior eye cups were flat-mounted onto slides (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) with the scleral side down using the SlowFade anti-fade mounting medium (Life Technologies). Fluorescent images were captured using an Axio Imager A2 microscope (Carl Zeiss, Oberkochen, Germany). Expression was quantified using ImageJ software (version 1.53, https://imagej.nih.gov/ij/index.html).

sec.title: Western blotting analysis
sec.p: Mice retina, RPE, and choroid were isolated via sonication in lysis buffer (iNtRON Biotechnology, Seongnam, Korea) and centrifuged at 13,000 rpm for 25 minutes at 4°C. Additionally, ARPE-19 cells were lysed using the iNtRON Biotechnology lysis buffer and centrifuged at 13,000 rpm for 20 minutes at 4°C. The supernatants were collected as the total protein extract. The proteins were transferred to PVDF membranes, which were blocked in 5% skim milk for 1 hour, and then incubated overnight at 4°C with the following antibodies: VEGFA (ab46154, 1:1,000; Abcam, Cambridge, UK), α-SMA (ab5694, 1:1,000; Abcam, Cambridge, UK), Cryab (ab13496, 1:2,500; Abcam, Cambridge, UK), p-Cryab (ser45) (PA1-011, 1:2,500; Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA), and GAPDH (2118S, 1:5,000; Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA). Thereafter, the blots were incubated with the corresponding conjugated goat anti-rabbit (7074S, 1:5,000; Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA) or horse anti-mouse IgG-HRP (7076S, 1:5,000; Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA) secondary antibodies.

sec.title: Molecular docking simulation
sec.p: The Maestro 13.1 program (Schrodinger, Inc., NY, USA) was used to predict the binding site using the induced fit docking protocol as previously described (Sherman et al., 2006). The binding of Cryab to Celafolin A-1, COFH5645, and COFH543435 was estimated based on its 3D structure, which was retrieved from the RCSB protein databank (PDB: 2W7J), and the structure of Celafolin A-1 was downloaded from PubChem (CID: 44593483). Cryab was protonated to add polar hydrogens and the structure was optimized and minimized using OPLS2005 force field. The optimal docked conformations of Celafolin A-1, COFH5645, and COFH543435 were determined based on glide energy, docking score, hydrogen bonds, and hydrophobic interactions. The conformations of Celafolin A-1, COFH5645, and COFH543435 were then docked to Cryab.

sec.title: Biolayer interferometry small molecule kinetic assay
sec.p: Biolayer interferometry (BLI) is a label-free optical technique that enables real-time analysis of biomolecular interactions by measuring changes in the interference pattern of white light reflected from a biosensor surface (Abdiche et al., 2008; Concepcion et al., 2009). In this study, BLI was employed using the Octet R4 system (Sartorius, Göttingen, Germany) along with Ni-NTA biosensors to assess the binding kinetics between Cryab and test compounds (Celafolin A-1, COFH5645, and COFH543435). The buffer used for the analysis contained PBS (0.0005% DMSO). The analysis was conducted with continuous shaking at 1,000 rpm at 30°C. Before analysis, Ni-NTA biosensors were hydrated in PBS for more than 10 min, followed by immobilization with 20 μg/mL His-tagged Cryab recombinant protein (NKMAX, Seongnam, Korea) for 1800 s. The analysis was conducted by sequentially increasing the concentration of the test compounds to 7.8125, 15.625, 31.25, 62.5, 125, 250, and 500 μM while performing association for a total of 180 s, followed by dissociation for 180 s. The Kd values for each compound were calculated using the 1:1 fit model with Octet software (Sartorius).

sec.title: Quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR)
sec.p: RNA was extracted from ARPE-19 cells using the QIAGEN RNA kit (QIAGEN, Hilden, Germany), and 1 μg of total RNA was reverse-transcribed into cDNA using the High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA). Amplification reactions were conducted using the StepOne Plus Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems) with 12.5 μL of 2×SYBR Green PCR master mix (Applied Biosystems), 1 μg of cDNA, and forward and reverse primers (100 μM each). Cycling parameters were as follows: 50°C for 2 min and 95°C for 10 min; 1 cycle at 95°C for 15 s and 40 cycles at 60°C for 2 min, after an initial step at 95°C for 30 s; and a final step at 55°C for 30 s. The primers used were as follows: Collagen I, forward 5′-TTGTGCGATGACGTGATCTGT-3′ and reverse 5′-TTGGTCGGTGGGTGACTCTG-3′; GAPDH, forward 5′-TGTCAAGCTCATTTCCTGGTATGA-3′ and reverse 5′-TCTTACTCCTTGGAGGCCATGTAG-3′.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by the Holm-Šídák post-hoc t-test, was performed using SigmaPlot 14 software (Systat Software, San Jose, CA, USA). The results are represented as mean ± standard error (SE). Statistical significance was set at p<0.05.

sec.title: RESULTS
Celafolin A-1 decreased the VEGF and α-SMA expression in vitro screening study
sec.p: Eight natural products were isolated from C. orbiculatus (Supplementary Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 1). The natural products were screened at 10 µM concentration. Four of the eight test compounds showed inhibitory effects on VEGF and α-SMA, greater than that of bevacizumab. This resulted in four hit compounds: Celafolin A-1, Celafolin D-3, COFH5645, and COFH543435 (Table 1). The IC50 values of the four compounds were determined. The most potent inhibitors were identified as Celafolin A-1, COFH5645, and COFH543435 (Table 2, Supplementary Fig. 2). These compounds were then studied in vivo.

sec.title: Celafolin A-1 decreased the hyper-reflective lesions in vivo
sec.p: In vivo analysis was conducted by comparing the hyperreflective lesions in laser-induced CNV mouse retinas treated with Celafolin A-1, COFH5645, and COFH543435. A hyperreflective lesion is a morphological feature observed on OCT as a hyperreflective material located within the RPE. The hyper-reflective lesion area in the Celafolin A-1 treatment group was significantly reduced compared to vehicle group, indicating a reduction in the pathological changes associated with CNV, while COFH5645 and COFH543435 treatments did not decrease the number of lesions [Fig. 1: F(3,37)=5.829, p=0.002]. These results suggest that Celafolin A-1 has a unique ability to reduce hyperreflective lesions in vivo.

sec.title: Celafolin A-1 decreased the CNV area in vivo
sec.p: The effect of Celafolin A-1, COFH5645, and COFH543435 on CNV area was assessed after a single bolus of the test compound was intravitreally administered to the mice. The CNV area was evaluated using isolectin B4 staining, which highlights the neovascularization within the retina. The CNV area in the Celafolin A-1 treatment group was significantly reduced compared to vehicle group, while treatments with COFH5645 and COFH543435 did not show a significant decrease [Fig. 2: F(3,31)=66.381, p=0.002]. These findings highlight the efficacy of Celafolin A-1 in targeting and reducing CNV in vivo.

sec.title: Celafolin A-1 decreased VEGFA and α-SMA expression in vivo
sec.p: VEGFA is a critical factor in promoting neovascularization, while α-SMA is a marker of fibrosis. Protein extracts from retina-RPE-choroid complex of mice’ eyes were analyzed to measure the expression levels of these markers. Celafolin A-1 treatment resulted in a significant reduction in the expression levels of both VEGFA and α-SMA, suggesting that it effectively inhibits both neovascularization and fibrotic processes in vivo, while COFH5645 and COFH543435 did not significantly affect the expression levels of these markers [Fig. 3A: F(4,15)=7.666, p=0.011; Fig. 3B: F(4,27)=3.915, p=0.012]. These results suggest the dual-action potential of Celafolin A-1 in addressing both angiogenic and fibrotic pathways.

sec.title: Celafolin A-1 and Cryab in silico binding prediction
sec.p: Cryab has been reported to stabilize VEGF and promote fibrosis (Ishikawa et al., 2016; Kase et al., 2010), while Celafolin A-1 possesses a cinnamic acid moiety implicated in protein interactions (Bai et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025). Therefore, we hypothesized that Celafolin A-1 might directly interact with Cryab. To investigate the potential interaction between Celafolin A-1 and Cryab, molecular docking simulations were performed. Receptor and ligand preparations were conducted using Schrödinger’s Protein Preparation Wizard and LigPrep, respectively. The docking score was measured as –3.962. Cryab and Celafolin A-1 binding sites were predicted as follows: HID 48 [B], MET 3 [A], PHE 55 [B], ARG 57 [A], where [A] is chain A and [B] is chain B of Cryab (Fig. 4A, 4B). To further elucidate the structural determinants of binding specificity, we compared the chemical structure of Celafolin A-1 with those of the non-binding analogs, COFH5645 and COFH543435 (Fig. 4C-4E). The molecular docking analysis of Celafolin A-1 identified a interaction between its cinnamoyl group and the PHE 55 [B] residue of Cryab. However, the structural comparison reveals that both COFH5645 and COFH543435 lack this essential cinnamoyl moiety. Consequently, these compounds failed to yield any convergent docking poses in the simulation, confirming that the cinnamoyl-mediated interaction is a prerequisite for stable binding to Cryab.

sec.title: In vitro binding assay with biolayer interferometry system
sec.p: Based on in silico predictions suggesting that Celafolin A-1 could bind to Cryab, we performed real-time binding affinity measurements using the Octet biolayer interferometry system. The analysis confirmed a specific interaction between Celafolin A-1 and Cryab, with a dissociation constant (Kd) of 163.6 µM and a coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.8561. This binding affinity indicates a moderate but specific interaction. In contrast, no significant interactions were observed between Cryab and the other two test compounds, COFH5645 and COFH543435 (Fig. 5, Table 1). These findings suggest that the binding of Celafolin A-1 to Cryab may be a critical mechanism underlying its therapeutic effects (Supplementary Fig. 3).

sec.title: Celafolin A-1 reduced the expression levels of Cryab and collagen I in ARPE-19 cells
sec.p: In vitro studies were conducted to further investigate the effects of Celafolin A-1 on Cryab and collagen I expression in ARPE-19 cells. These cells were stimulated with TCM (THP-1 conditional media) to induce stress responses, mimicking the pathological environment of CNV. Celafolin A-1 treatment significantly decreased the expression of Cryab and collagen I in TCM-stimulated ARPE-19 cells (Fig. 6A: F(3,20)=18.157, p<0.001; Fig. 6B: F(3,12)=6.908, p=0.006). The maximum effect was observed with 600 nM of Celafolin A-1. These results support the anti-fibrotic potential of Celafolin A-1, as it effectively downregulates fibrosis-related proteins in vitro.

sec.title: Celafolin A-1 reduced Cryab and p-Cryab (ser45) expression in vivo
sec.p: We evaluated the effect of Celafolin A-1 on the expression of Cryab and p-Cryab (Ser45) in a laser-induced CNV mouse model using western blotting. Phosphorylation of Cryab is associated with its chaperone activity and stress response functions. Total Cryab protein was reduced in Celafolin A-1–treated eyes compared with the vehicle control group (Fig. 7: F(2,17)=5.383, p=0.0154). The expression of the cleaved form of p-Cryab (Ser45) was significantly decreased in the eyes of Celafolin A-1-treated mice compared to the control group (Fig. 7: F(2,9)=13.505, p=0.002). This reduction suggests that Celafolin A-1 modulates Cryab activity and potentially mitigates its pro-fibrotic effects. Taken together, these findings indicate that Celafolin A-1 decreases total Cryab expression both in vitro and in vivo, and additionally reduces the phosphorylated cleaved form of Cryab in vivo under disease conditions.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: Anti-VEGF therapeutics, including bevacizumab, aflibercept, and ranibizumab, constitute the primary pharmacological modality for managing nAMD, primarily targeting the suppression of pathological neovascularization (Malik et al., 2014). Despite their clinical efficacy in inhibiting abnormal vascular proliferation, a significant and persistent challenge in the prognosis of nAMD patients is the development of subretinal fibrosis following anti-angiogenic treatment. Studies have demonstrated that approximately 45% of patients develop fibrotic scarring within two years of initiating anti-VEGF monotherapy (Daniel et al., 2014), highlighting the critical role of fibrotic scarring for vision loss in nAMD patients (Flores et al., 2021). The absence of effective anti-fibrotic agents for nAMD further complicates treatment outcomes, necessitating novel therapeutic strategies. In this study, we employed an in vitro screening approach to identify three promising compounds for the treatment of nAMD. Among these, Celafolin A-1 emerged as the most effective in ameliorating hyperreflective lesions and fibrosis in a laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (CNV) mouse model. Specifically, Celafolin A-1 administration resulted in a significant reduction of laser-induced CNV lesions following a single intravitreal injection, accompanied by decreased expression of VEGF and α-SMA, which are essential markers of neovascularization and fibrosis, respectively. Further mechanistic investigations were conducted to elucidate the effects of Celafolin A-1 on ARPE-19 cells. Celafolin A-1 significantly attenuated the upregulation of VEGF, α-SMA, and collagen I expression-induced by TCM. In vivo, Celafolin A-1 inhibited the expression of Cryab and cleaved form of p-Cryab (ser45) in a laser-induced CNV mouse model.

A critical finding of this study is the specific binding affinity of Celafolin A-1 to Cryab (Kd ≈ 163.6 µM). While this affinity is in the moderate range, it characterizes Celafolin A-1 as a promising hit compound. Importantly, this binding was sufficient to elicit a potent in vivo phenotype in our CNV model, validating its potential as a scaffold for further optimization. In contrast, the other two compounds, COFH5645 and COFH543435, did not exhibit binding to Cryab in either in silico simulations or biolayer interferometry binding affinity assays. The unique presence of a cinnamoyl group in Celafolin A-1 was predicted to facilitate binding to PHE55 [B], consistent with known anti-inflammatory (Nair et al., 2022) and anti-fibrotic (Abdalhameid et al., 2024) properties of cinnamic acid and its derivatives. These derivatives also exhibit vascular inhibition effects through the regulation of pancreatic β-cells, contributing to their anti-diabetic effects (Adisakwattana, 2017).

The role of Cryab in nAMD pathogenesis is complex and involves multiple pathways. Cryab enhances the structural stability of VEGF, a critical factor in pathological angiogenesis (Kase et al., 2010), and functions as a co-regulator of α-SMA (Yu et al., 2022). Therefore, inhibition of Cryab expression by Celafolin A-1 is expected to reduce VEGF stability, accelerate its degradation, and ultimately lower its functional availability. Deficiency in Cryab correlates with reduced activity of α-SMA and collagen I (Bellaye et al., 2014), indicating its involvement in subretinal fibrosis and CNV progression. Cryab’s phosphorylation sites regulate its chaperone activity (Ecroyd et al., 2007) suggesting its significant role in nAMD pathogenesis. The observed decrease in the phosphorylated cleaved form of Cryab at Ser45 in vivo supports the involvement of post-translational regulation. In addition, Cryab functions as an oligomeric chaperone, forming dimers and higher-order assemblies that help prevent protein aggregation (Hayashi and Carver, 2020; Peschek et al., 2013; Sprague-Piercy et al., 2021). When oligomer stability is disturbed, Cryab can become aggregation-prone, as observed with the D109A mutation that reduces oligomerization in myofibrillar myopathy (Fichna et al., 2017). In light of this evidence, it is possible that Celafolin A-1 lowers Cryab activity not only by reducing its protein level but also by affecting its oligomerization, which could weaken its normal structure and function. Clinical investigations have further demonstrated increased Cryab expression in AMD patient samples, including RPE cells adjacent to drusen and hypertrophic RPE in nAMD (De et al., 2007). In our previous study, vitreous levels of Cryab were significantly elevated in patients with rhegmatogenous retinal detachment complicated by proliferative vitreoretinopathy which is also associated with fibrosis (Yun and Min, 2020). Moreover, our proteomics analysis of aqueous humor from nAMD patients identified Cryab as one of the most significantly upregulated proteins, reinforcing its role as a clinically relevant mediator in retinal angiogenesis and fibrosis (Yu et al., 2024). Collectively, these studies support the clinical relevance of Cryab as a biomarker and therapeutic target in retinal disease.

Although Celafolin A-1 directly binds to Cryab as confirmed by BLI analysis, this interaction alone is unlikely to fully account for its therapeutic efficacy. Alternative mechanisms may involve indirect modulation of Cryab expression, phosphorylation, and cleavage, as well as Cryab-independent pathways. Our previous work demonstrated that AIF, despite being structurally distinct, indirectly downregulates Cryab by attenuating oxidative stress- and inflammation-mediated pathways (Yu et al., 2022). In contrast, Celafolin A-1 directly binds to Cryab, as confirmed by our BLI analysis, and modulates its phosphorylation, thereby exerting a more direct regulatory effect. These complementary mechanisms highlight how structurally unrelated compounds can converge on Cryab regulation and provide therapeutic benefit by suppressing both angiogenesis and fibrosis in nAMD.

Furthermore, given that the NF-κB pathway which is inhibited by C. orbiculatus plays a central role not only in inflammation but also in VEGF expression (Qian et al., 2012) and epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), a key mediator of fibrosis (Wang et al., 2023), Celafolin A-1 may exert part of its therapeutic effects through modulation of this pathway. Importantly, EMT in RPE cells has been recognized as a fundamental mechanism driving subretinal fibrogenesis in nAMD (Tamiya et al., 2010). Thus, the ability of Celafolin A-1 to attenuate NF-κB signaling provides a mechanistic basis for its observed anti-angiogenic and anti-fibrotic activities. Taken together, these results suggest that Celafolin A-1 exerts its therapeutic activity through both direct interaction with Cryab and complementary indirect mechanisms. The development of Celafolin A-1 as an effective therapeutic agent for nAMD not only requires understanding its interactions with Cryab but also involves elucidating its impact on various signaling pathways. The inhibition of VEGF and α-SMA suggests that Celafolin A-1 may interfere with the signaling cascades involved in angiogenesis and fibrogenesis. VEGF is known to play a pivotal role in neovascularization, while α-SMA is a marker for myofibroblast differentiation, which is crucial in the process of fibrosis (Little et al., 2018). By downregulating these markers, Celafolin A-1 potentially inhibits the pathological progression of both neovascularization and fibrosis in nAMD.

Despite the promising outcomes presented here, several limitations should be considered. First, although the laser-induced CNV mouse model is widely used and recapitulates certain aspects of human nAMD, it does not fully reflect the chronic and multifactorial nature of the disease. Second, the present work did not address the long-term efficacy and safety of Celafolin A-1, which are critical considerations for its potential clinical translation. Third, while our findings highlight Cryab as a key molecular target, the downstream signaling pathways by which Cryab contributes to angiogenesis and fibrosis remain incompletely understood. Future studies should therefore focus on evaluating the durability and safety of Celafolin A-1 in extended preclinical settings, as well as elucidating the Cryab-mediated signaling cascades that underlie its therapeutic effects. Additionally, future pharmacokinetic studies are necessary to determine the half-life and retinal retention of Celafolin A-1 following intravitreal injection. Such efforts will provide deeper mechanistic insights and further validate the translational potential of Celafolin A-1 as a dual-action therapy for nAMD.

In conclusion, Celafolin A-1 exhibits potential as a novel therapeutic agent for nAMD by targeting fibrosis, a major limitation of current anti-VEGF therapies. These results support further research to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying Celafolin A-1’s effects, and to evaluate its long-term efficacy and safety in preclinical settings. Our study provides a basis for developing Celafolin A-1 as a dual-action therapeutic agent, addressing both neovascular and fibrotic components of nAMD (Fig. 8).

caption.p: Inhibitory effects of Celafolin A-1, COFH5645, and COFH543435 on hyper-reflective lesion expression in the laser-induced CNV mice. The hyper-reflective lesion area was significantly decreased after Celafolin A-1 intravitreal administration. However, COFH5645 and COFH543435 did not decrease the hyper-reflective lesions. In OCT images, red dotted lines denote the lesion areas. Corresponding lesion sites are indicated by white dotted circles in the fundus photographs. Eyes with anomalous structures, cataract, or visible defects of the cornea or fundus were excluded. Data were analyzed using a one-way ANOVA followed by the Holm-Šídák post-hoc t-test (##p<0.01 vs. vehicle group), and the results are expressed as mean ± SE (n=7-15). The scale bar in each image is 200 μm.

Inhibitory effect of Celafolin A-1 on the CNV area in a mouse model of laser-induced CNV. The CNV area was analyzed by measuring the fluorescence intensity of images containing an isolectin B4 positive area. White dotted lines denote the lesion areas. Eyes with anomalous structures, cataract, or visible defects of the cornea or fundus were excluded. Data were analyzed using a one-way ANOVA followed by the Holm-Šídák post-hoc t-test (##p<0.01 vs. vehicle group). The results are expressed as mean ± SE. (n=6-11). The scale bar in each image is 100 μm.

Celafolin A-1 inhibits the expression of VEGFA and α-SMA in a laser-induced CNV mouse model. (A) VEGFA and (B) α-SMA expressions were markedly elevated in the vehicle group compared with the naïve group. Intravitreal administration of 5 mg/mL Celafolin A-1 significantly reduced the expression of both markers whereas treatment with COFH5645 or COFH543435 resulted in no significant reduction in VEGFA or α-SMA expression. Eyes with anomalous structures, cataract, or visible defects of the cornea or fundus were excluded. Data were analyzed using a one-way ANOVA followed by the Holm-Šídák post-hoc t-test (*p<0.05 vs. non-laser exposed group and #p<0.05 vs. vehicle group) and the results are expressed as mean ± SE (n=4-8). The original blots are presented in Supplementary Fig. 4.

The predicted binding of Celafolin A-1 to Cryab and structural comparison. (A) Identification of Cryab and Celafolin A-1 binding sites through molecular modeling. Zoom-in view highlighting the hydrophobic interaction between the cinnamoyl group of Celafolin A-1 and the PHE 55 [B] residue (red dashed lines). (B) Through the ligand interaction diagram, Cryab and Celafolin A-1 binding sites were predicted as follows: HID 48 [B], MET 3 [A], PHE 55 [B], and ARG 57 [A]. However, COFH5645 and COFH543435 did not bind to Cryab. (C-E) Chemical structures of (C) Celafolin A-1, (D) COFH5645, and (E) COFH543435, with the cinnamoyl moiety in Celafolin A-1 highlighted in green.

Celafolin A-1 directly binds to Cryab. The binding affinity between test compounds and Cryab was measured using a biolayer interferometry Octet system, which is based on biolayer interferometry technology. The binding affinity Kd value between Celafolin A-1 and Cryab was 163.6 µM. Binding response of different concentrations of (A) Celafolin A-1, (B) COFH5645, and (C) COFH543435 was measured using the biolayer interferometry Octet R4 system.

Celafolin A-1 inhibits the expression of Cryab and collagen I in ARPE-19 cells. (A) ARPE-19 cells were treated with 300 or 600 nM Celafolin A-1 and analyzed using western blotting (n=6). (B) ARPE-19 cells were treated with 600 nM Celafolin A-1, and mRNA expression was assessed. Celafolin A-1 reduced the expression levels of Cryab and collagen I at 600 nM (n=4). Data were analyzed using a one-way ANOVA followed by the Holm-Šídák post-hoc t-test (**p<0.01 vs. control group, #p<0.05 and ##p<0.01 vs. only TCM group), and the results are expressed as mean ± SE. The original blots are presented in Supplementary Fig. 5.

Inhibitory effects of Celafolin A-1 on Cryab and phosphorylated-Cryab (p-Cryab) expression in a laser-induced CNV model. Immediately following laser exposure, intravitreal injection of Celafolin A-1 at a concentration of 5 mg/mL was administered. The expression of the cleaved form of p-Cryab (ser45) was decreased by Celafolin A-1 at a concentration of 5 mg/mL. Total Cryab was also reduced in the treated group. Eyes with anomalous structures, cataract, or visible defects of the cornea or fundus were excluded. Data were analyzed using one-way ANOVA followed by the Holm-Šídák post-hoc t-test (*p<0.05 and **p<0.01 vs. naïve group, #p<0.05 vs. vehicle group) and the results are expressed as mean ± SE (n=4-8). The original blots are presented in Supplementary Fig. 6.

Schematic illustration of the proposed dual-action mechanism of Celafolin A-1 in nAMD. Celafolin A-1 specifically binds to Cryab and directly inhibits its phosphorylation at Ser45 (solid lines). This blockade leads to a loss of chaperone function, which triggers two key downstream pathways (dashed lines). Protein destabilization of VEGF, resulting in the suppression of angiogenesis, and downregulation of α-SMA protein expression, leading to the inhibition of fibrosis. Consequently, Celafolin A-1 effectively ameliorates the pathological progression of nAMD by targeting both neovascular and fibrotic components. The illustration was created with Biorender.com. nAMD, neovascular age-related macular degeneration; CRYAB, crystallin alpha B; VEGF, vascular endothelial growth factor; α-SMA, alpha-smooth muscle actin.
